item.title: The Psychology of True Crime and Emotional Regulation
item.description:
Law and Crime

The Psychology of True Crime and Emotional Regulation

True crime may reduce symptoms of anxiety, fear, and insecurity.

Posted August 14, 2026

Key points
  • Participants who felt more anxious one day tend to consume more violent true crime the next day.
  • The more violent the true crime, the better their likelihood of being in a good mood the next day.
  • True crime doesn't increase consumers' anxiety or level of fear.
  • Consuming true crime before bedtime often results in less anxiety the following day.
Source: RDNE / Pexels

Is exposure to true crime a threat to our mental health or a potential coping skill?

A 2025 study by Perchtold-Stefan, Rominger, and Fink attempted to answer the question of whether the experience of watching, reading, or listening to true crime increases negative affect—such as anxiety, fear, and insecurity—or if people who experience anxiety, fear, and insecurity are more likely to gravitate to true crime media.

This study surveyed a sample population of 199 German adults, each of whom kept a daily diary of their consumption of both true crime and fictional crime. Daily diary designs are often considered the gold standard of data collection because they capture data in real time rather than relying on memory, which may be biased.

Participants also kept track of their mood in terms of positive affect (interested, excited, strong, enthusiastic, proud, alert, inspired, determined, attentive, active) and negative affect (distressed, upset, guilty, scared, hostile, irritable, ashamed, nervous, jittery, afraid). Responses concerning negative affect were divided into two different categories: those who experienced anxiety (feelings of being “scared,” “nervous,” and “afraid”) and those who experienced anger (feeling “upset,” “hostile,” and “irritable”).

For two weeks, study participants were asked to report on the following questions:

  1. Did you consume any true crime today, and if so, in what format (i.e., books, television, podcasts, news broadcasts)?
  2. For how many minutes did you consume true crime?
  3. How violent was the true crime you consumed on a scale of one to five, with five being the most violent?
  4. Are you planning to consume true crime today before going to sleep?

Results

Your level of anxiety predicts the quantity of true crime you consume.

Participants who felt more anxious one day tend to consume more violent true crime the next day. This suggests that people who struggle with anxiety may seek out the roller coaster of emotions that exposure to true crime brings—at least from the comfort of their own home, that is. It almost seems like anxious people are preparing for unknown dangers that they fear may lie hidden in their future.

The violence of the true crime you consume is related to a more positive mood on the following day, and the more violent the true crime you are exposed to, the better your likelihood of being in a good mood the following day.

I know, I know, this might sound like a concerning finding. But before you start suspecting your friend, neighbor, or spouse of being a sociopath, let’s take this scientific finding apart.

For many people—especially those struggling with anxiety—preparation for the worst-case scenario may be their only defense against the irrational or unrealistic fears that plague them. Exposure to true crime may offer some people a sense of control or mastery by imagining what they would do in certain dangerous and terrifying scenarios.

Imagine it sort of like a crime scene fire drill for your brain of the worst thing you can possibly come across. This preparation eases anxiety and taps into the psychological qualities of mastery and competence that make us feel stronger, more powerful, and more in control of a frightening situation.

True crime exposure does not increase anxiety, anger, or negative affect the day after consumption.

The assumption that consuming violent media increases fear and/or aggression was not supported by the findings of this study, although it is important to note that this study was made up of adult participants with an average age of 23.33 years, as opposed to children and adolescents who may be more susceptible to peer pressure and other outside influences on their underdeveloped brains.

People who consume true crime before they go to sleep tend to be less anxious the next day.

The relationship between consuming true crime before sleep and experiencing lower anxiety the following day is likely an example of a phenomenon called anticipatory emotional regulation. In layman’s terms, this means that some individuals may use familiar frightening narratives as a calming ritual.

If this sounds bizarre or counterintuitive, I’d like to remind you of some rather frightening stories we tell small children before bed including: a story in which a young blonde-haired girl is trapped inside a house with three angry bears, a child whose father dies suddenly, leaving her in the care of a cold, calculated stepmother and some vindictive half-siblings who take all of her belongings and try to steal her boyfriend, and an inadequately supervised brother and sister who go for a walk in the woods and meet an old woman who tries to eat them.

Conclusion

Exposure to true crime isn’t a type of treatment or therapy, but it may be helpful in reducing symptoms of anxiety, fear, and insecurity in a way that mimics the cognitive behavioral concept of exposure therapy. Exposure therapy is often used to decrease or eliminate phobias by having individuals slowly acclimate to a situation that has previously made them anxious. For example, someone with a fear or phobia of dogs might be shown a picture of a dog or asked to hold a dog leash as a stepping point to increase their level of tolerance for the fear they feel around dogs. Eventually, they can increase their tolerance to a point where they feel comfortable with having a dog in the room with them. Similarly, it appears that for some people, exposure to true crime may decrease their anxiety by making them feel less out of control if a danger does arise.

item.title: Your Quiet Child May Be the Most Overwhelmed
item.description:
Parenting

Your Quiet Child May Be the Most Overwhelmed

Why silence, withdrawal, and “I don't care” can be hidden signs of reactivity

Posted August 14, 2026

Key points
  • Reactivity isn’t always loud; silence or withdrawal can signal emotional overload.
  • Shutdown is easy to misread as stubbornness, avoidance, or indifference.
  • Withdrawing children often need space and curiosity more than pressure.

When I reflect on how parents often describe a “reactive child,” they usually describe noise. I’m talking about yelling, crying, doors slamming, throwing something. You get the picture. In short, when things melt down, everyone in the house knows it’s happening. But my point in writing this article is that some of the most overwhelmed kids I’ve worked with barely make a sound.

When kids go quiet, it may be in response to a parent asking about a failed test, and then the child stares at the floor. Or, a teenager gets embarrassed at a family gathering and suddenly stops talking. Or another scenario is a child struggling with homework who puts down the pencil or pulls the top down on their laptop, crosses their arms, and seemingly refuses to move. Inwardly, as I have written in many other posts here, these kids are often overthinking. They are second-guessing themselves and have anxiety over making mistakes.

The more complicated problems arise when adults understandably misinterpret what they see: She’s being stubborn. He’s shutting me out. She doesn’t care. Yet that outward quiet shutdown is often not seen as reflecting emotionally loud pain within the child’s mind.

Emotional Reactivity Has More Than One Face

A child’s nervous system can respond to feeling overwhelmed in several ways. Some children become explosive, where they get louder, faster, and more physical. Others shut down, as seen when they withdraw, refuse, or stop responding. Still others freeze: their face goes blank, their body becomes still, and they seem almost eerily unaffected. Ironically, that third child may receive the least support because adults assume nothing is happening.

This quieter side of reactivity (as well as the loud, in-your-face meltdowns) is something I explore in 24 Hours to a Less Reactive Child: The One-Day Reset to Reduce Conflict, Calm Big Emotions, and Reconnect. One of the central ideas is that parents can become so focused on problematic behavior that they miss what happened immediately before it—the internal emotional surge. And when the behavior is almost invisible, the surge is especially easy to miss.

Some Practical Examples of What Parents Can Say to Help

Here are some examples of what parents can say in emotionally reactivity-driven shutdown situations with kids across a range of ages. In each of these examples, consider how parents respond in a calm, supportive manner to help reduce their kid’s reactivity.

Age 7

Joey is staring off, visibly resistant to doing his homework. He becomes very quiet and appears stressed.

Do not say: “You’re just sitting there. Pick up the pencil.”

Instead say: “Something about this feels really hard right now. Just know I’m here to help you want to draw a picture about how you feel, or we can talk about it.”

Age 13

Bella suddenly falls silent after being embarrassed by a group text from her friends that are writing about her being too sensitive about some teasing she experienced earlier that day in school.

Do not say: “Why are you moping about this and being so dramatic? I’m sure this will all blow over tomorrow.”

Instead say: “You got really quiet. I’ll give you some space, and I’m here to listen if you’d like to talk about it.”

Age 17

Abe says the dreaded “I don’t care” when he finds out he was cut from the school soccer team.

Do not say: “Obviously you do care, so stop pretending you don’t.”

Instead, say: “You don’t have to talk about it right now. We can come back to it if that will feel helpful to you.”

Some Final Thoughts

Navigating a child who is reacting within and appears outwardly silent and shut down can be very trying for parents. None of those samples of responses mean accepting disrespect, abandoning expectations, or diagnosing every quiet moment as emotional distress.

They mean becoming curious before becoming corrective. I can’t stress enough the power of gentle curiosity vs. making judgmental, corrective suggestions when engaging emotionally reacting kids. And keep in mind that parents naturally notice the child who turns the emotional volume up. The greater challenge may be noticing the child whose nervous system turns everything down. Sometimes the kid creating the least disturbance in the room is the one working hardest to hold themselves together. Based on working with these kids in my office and coaching their parents, I have seen just how much they value your emotional support when it’s delivered in a way that feels safe for them to process.

item.title: The Inevitability of the Extreme
item.description:
Social Life

The Inevitability of the Extreme

Bad (or good) outomes can occur without bad (or good) causes in play.

Posted August 14, 2026

Key points
  • Extremism is troubling, especially in the socio-political world.
  • Many troubling phenomena have equally troubling causes.
  • Extremism can also rise from more innocuous origins.

The number 18 is surely extreme. – Hoca Camide, trying to make an incontestable point.

Adeo causa non deest [There’s no shortage of causes] – Pliny the Elder

Source: AndriiKoval/Shutterstock

Visegrád is a village near the knee of the Danube. Rising in the west, the great river flows past Vienna to become Hungary’s border with Slovakia. Rolling past Visegrád and the hilltop Plintenburg, the river then makes a 90-degree turn to head South toward Budapest. In the Slavonic language, “Visegrád” means High (Vise) Castle (Grád). It is a beautiful, if Kafkaesque, setting. Down by the river, we find a swanky wellness hotel with baths, a bar, and conference rooms. It was here that we, a small group of psychologists and other social scientists, shared our thoughts on the psychology of extremism, a topic for our time. It was then and there that I realized that my views on the matter were rather moderate.

The group shared a broad consensus that extremism, and political extremism in particular, is a social phenomenon with potentially corrosive consequences. This is not an extreme attitude to have. Worries about political extremism are de rigueur and received as socially responsible (Freilich et al., 2024). Political extremism is a contributing factor to intolerance, aggression, and even violence. There is a good deal of empirical evidence for the link between extremism and aggression, but it is also clear that extreme political attitudes do not necessarily produce violence. It is perfectly possible to entertain extreme viewpoints without engaging in destructive behavior.

The scientist’s job is to detect, to explain, and (perhaps) to advise on a phenomenon of interest. So, we asked how we know whether a position is extreme, whether we can account for its origins, and what might be done to mitigate the detrimental consequences that might ensue. As to detection, a perception of extremity requires a distribution of data, that is, referents for comparison (extremus = the outermost). The extremity of the number 18 is indeterminate. If it is the number of years lived at the time of death, 18 is extremely small; if it is the number of children begotten by a loving couple, it is extremely large. Psychologically speaking, judgments of extremity either require extensional (i.e., distributional) knowledge (i.e., experience) or implicit assumptions, however hallucinatory, about things not seen. No stimulus stands alone.

As to causation, the search for origins is driven by observed or assumed consequences. Having agreed that extremism is bad, people—and the scientists who study it—readily assume that causes resemble their consequences. In particular, bad consequences are thought to follow bad causes. This bias is known as immanent justice reasoning in moral psychology (Callan et al., 2014), and it resembles the workings of the representativeness heuristic (Kahneman & Tversky, 1972). Hence, the symposiasts at Hotel Visegrád naturally attributed political extremism to conspiracy cognition, personal and collective narcissism, shallow causal reasoning, mean leaders, and of course, the terrors of social media.

I believe all these causal stories have merit, but I doubt that these stories are the whole story. There is plenty of evidence from psychology and other sciences for the idea that systems (including political systems) can drift or shift into extreme states. A tiny disruption of a fragile equilibrium of counterbalancing forces can be enough. What is true for climate change can also apply to attitude change. A well-ordered republic comprises a diversity of viewpoints, which necessitate one another and keep one another in check. Those on the right or on the left may not fully realize how their views receive meaning and validity only by virtue of being situated within the same system with those whom they so energetically oppose.

In the political world, the notion of an equilibrium means that the right won’t become more right and that the left won’t become more left in the course of events. Likewise, equilibrium means that the right and the left will not collapse into a grand consensus, thereby ending their energetic disputes and turn-taking in political power. A symmetrical increase in extreme positions can preserve the equilibrium, at least for a time, while eroding the common ground both sides rely on for their functioning.

Most thinkers, writers, scholars, and scientists engaging with the issue of extremism are, I believe, worried about disruptions of the political equilibrium by asymmetrical increases. A natural bias is to detect increases in extremism on the other side, away from one’s own. Extreme attitudes are the attitudes we discern among those who disagree with us (Dawes et al., 1972; Ross et al., 1977). Only a true moderate would be equally worried about the far right and the far left; but then, whose views are located precisely in the middle of the spectrum? What is more, if there is a greater growth of extreme attitudes on one side than on the other, the point of true moderation will shift as well (Parducci, 1965).

There are alternatives to the grim view that bad consequences must have bad causes (Krueger & Aizenberg, in press). One such alternative is that extreme positions yield confidence and a sense of identity simply by virtue of being rare. Extremists own their views even if they are hard-pressed to explain them (Fernbach et al., 2013). Half-range views smack of indifference, ignorance, or both (Goldberg, 1981). Again, we must note the role of opposing forces in a well-balanced system. Although extreme positions can be appealing, people might also be scared of them. They seek out the middle, or middling, ground as a hiding place. A person who has no view cannot be challenged on substantive grounds (Hollingsworth, 1910).

Another alternative is that random sampling observations and experiences will increase the range and the (uncorrected) variance of the data, though slowly so when samples become large (Tippett, 1925). Very large or very small values are improbable in small samples, but virtually assured in very large samples. In the absence of compensating centripetal forces, it is more likely to find extremists in large than in small groups. The same logic holds within a person. The longer we live and the more we experience, the more likely it is that we sample something from the edge of the imaginable. This is one good reason to keep living: we do not know what we have not seen yet (Krueger, 2018).

These ideas are not meant to make light of the problems that come with extreme social views, especially views that are intolerant of dissent. Rather, this essay is meant to be a note of caution. Extreme views do not necessarily signal the presence of extreme (and unsavory) causes.
